short: The PostgreSQL server process that runs statements for a client connection.
detail: A backend changes pages in shared buffers and inserts WAL records. It can perform WAL flushes or write a dirty eviction victim on the foreground path.
design: Buffer misses and slow storage can increase query latency even when client CPU usage is low.

short: The common pool of cached data-file pages used by PostgreSQL processes.
detail: Each frame can hold one block from a heap or index. Processes share access to cached blocks. Writes usually dirty the frame in memory and let another process write it later.
design: Size for the workload and account for the OS page cache. A larger pool can reduce eviction but may leave more dirty data for checkpoints.

short: A block of table storage. A buffer is dirty after changes that still need writing.
detail: PostgreSQL usually uses 8 KiB pages. A dirty buffer can be written even if the transaction that changed it is still open, as long as the WAL describing the change is durable.
design: A clean buffer is cheap to evict. A shortage of clean buffers can put writes on an application request’s critical path.

short: Shared memory used to assemble records in the write-ahead log before writing them to disk.
detail: WAL records describe page changes, commits and other events. WAL insertion, write to the operating system, and flush to durable storage are separate milestones.
design: Distinguish WAL generation from storage flush latency. Increasing WAL buffer space cannot make the device flush faster.

short: A background process that periodically writes and flushes WAL.
detail: An asynchronous commit may wake it. Backends can flush WAL directly for synchronous commits. In PostgreSQL the documented async risk window can be up to three times wal_writer_delay.
design: For transactions that need durable acknowledgements, choose synchronous_commit. Changing writer timing only changes the window of exposure.

short: The background writer prepares clean, reusable buffers in advance of demand.
detail: It estimates upcoming buffer allocations from recent activity and writes some dirty eviction candidates. bgwriter_lru_maxpages controls how many it can write per round.
design: More proactive writes can reduce foreground stalls at the cost of rewriting hot buffers that get dirty again.

short: The checkpointer establishes a recovery starting point and makes earlier changes durable in the data files.
detail: It chooses a REDO point, writes and syncs the required data, and persists a checkpoint record. pg_control is updated after the record is durable. Concurrent writes can leave pages dirty again.
design: Checkpoint scheduling trades recovery time against foreground I/O, WAL volume, and the disk space needed before old segments can be recycled.

short: The local directory containing durable WAL and the segment files used to write it.
detail: WAL is divided into fixed-size segment files, normally 16 MiB each. Checkpoints can recycle old files once crash recovery, replication and archiving no longer need them. This lab uses 32 KiB segments.
design: Budget for retention blockers separately from max_wal_size. A slot or failed archiver can grow the directory beyond that target.

short: The files that hold table and index blocks.
detail: Data-file blocks can lag changes already recorded durably in WAL. Checkpoint completion guarantees the on-disk files are sufficient for restart from the chosen REDO point.
design: Budget write bandwidth for pages as well as sequential WAL, especially when a write-heavy workload dirties a broad working set.

short: The cluster control file that tells startup which checkpoint to use.
detail: The control file stores the last completed checkpoint location and a copy of checkpoint metadata. Startup uses the checkpoint’s REDO pointer to find the start of the recovery scan.
design: An in-progress checkpoint cannot shorten the next restart. Recovery depends on a usable checkpoint and the WAL it requires.

short: Reapplying logged changes in order after a crash or on a standby.
detail: Redo restores applicable full-page images and checks page LSNs before replaying ordinary deltas. Crash recovery scans to the end of valid WAL.
design: Measure recovery under realistic WAL backlog and I/O. A database that survives crashes may still miss its recovery-time target.

short: On-disk transaction status used to decide whether a transaction committed.
detail: Formerly pg_clog, it stores commit and abort status. Redo can reconstruct committed status from WAL. An interrupted transaction can leave physical changes, but without durable commit status its changes stay invisible.
design: Physical page state and transaction visibility are different layers. A flushed heap page is no evidence that its transaction committed.

short: A primary-side process that streams WAL to a connected standby.
detail: A physical walsender sends WAL from the standby’s requested position and tracks its feedback. On a primary it sends locally flushed WAL.
design: Compare local flush with sent LSN before blaming replay. Sender backlog and replay backlog point to different bottlenecks.

short: The standby process that receives streaming WAL and writes it locally.
detail: It reports write and flush progress. The standby startup process applies WAL and reports replay progress separately.
design: A standby can durably receive writes faster than it applies them. Use replay progress to reason about stale reads.

short: A persistent retention record for a particular WAL consumer.
detail: A slot holds the WAL its consumer might still need, even when disconnected. Physical slots serve standbys. Logical slots support decoding and can also retain catalog history.
design: Own each slot’s lifecycle and alert on retained bytes. An abandoned slot can take the producer database down by consuming its WAL disk.

short: The command PostgreSQL runs to copy a completed WAL segment to archival storage.
detail: When archiving is enabled, unarchived complete segments are retained until the copy reports success. The destination must preserve and verify each segment so the chain can be restored.
design: Monitor success age and the unarchived backlog. A failing archive can exhaust pg_wal even when every replica is caught up.

short: WAL for a page change must be durable before PostgreSQL writes that data page.
detail: The buffer writer flushes WAL through the page LSN if needed. This ordering lets recovery reconstruct updates even when the data-file page lags WAL.
design: Separating a small sequential durability write from later page writes keeps the synchronous commit path short while preserving recovery.

short: A byte position in the WAL stream.
detail: PostgreSQL displays a WAL position as two hexadecimal numbers separated by a slash. The difference between positions on the same timeline is the WAL bytes generated between them.
design: Measure lag and retention in bytes as well as time. Even a short stall can consume a large amount of disk during a write spike.

short: The WAL position associated with the most recent WAL-logged change reflected in a page.
detail: The page header stores the LSN. For an ordinary delta, redo can skip work if the page already has an equal or higher LSN. Applicable full-page images can restore a damaged page without trusting its header.
design: Page LSN checks make replay of ordinary deltas safe across pages that were flushed at different times.

short: A storage synchronization operation that makes already-written WAL durable.
detail: A regular write can finish while bytes remain in the OS cache. PostgreSQL’s wal_sync_method chooses the mechanism for making them persistent. The lab calls the simulated flush fsync.
design: Commit tail latency reflects the durability cost of the storage stack. Measure it separately from ordinary write throughput.

short: A WAL entry recording successful completion of a transaction.
detail: The commit record can be later in WAL than the records for the pages the transaction changed. On restart, the durable commit record lets redo recover committed status.
design: An observed heap change does not prove a durable transaction. Anchor guarantees and failure analysis to the commit record and client acknowledgement.

short: The transaction setting that decides how much WAL progress must occur before client OK.
detail: local requires primary flush. With a configured synchronous standby, on also requires standby flush and remote_apply waits for replay. The off setting permits early acknowledgement.
design: Choose guarantees per transaction where appropriate. Standby health becomes a write-latency dependency when its feedback is required.

short: Returning client OK before the primary has flushed the commit record.
detail: With synchronous_commit off, a crash can lose some recent acknowledged transactions. The write-ahead rule still holds, and redo ignores transactions whose commit records did not survive.
design: Reserve this durability trade-off for data that can be regenerated or lost within an explicit budget.

short: One WAL flush makes more than one concurrent commit durable.
detail: Several backends can wait for locations covered by the same flush. Commits/s is the average client OK rate through the last acknowledgement in the run, with a 100 ms minimum timing window in this lab.
design: Fsync latency and commits/s can move independently. Moderate concurrency can amortize a flush while single-request latency remains bound by storage.

short: A buffer replacement algorithm that gives recently used frames a second chance.
detail: The clock hand passes through frames. Unpinned frames with positive usage are aged by decrementing their count. An unpinned frame at zero can be reused after writing it if dirty.
design: Foreground writes under churn can inflate tail latency. Compare the active working set with the buffer footprint and examine reuse and write counters.

short: The WAL position at which recovery starts scanning for a completed checkpoint.
detail: An online checkpoint chooses this position when it starts. Its durable checkpoint record comes later, after writing and syncing the necessary data.
design: A server can crash during a checkpoint and still need all WAL from the previous REDO point. Keep enough storage for that overlap.

short: A copy of a page in WAL that recovery can use to replace an incomplete disk write.
detail: With full_page_writes enabled, the first WAL-logged change to an ordinary page after a new REDO point usually records an image. PostgreSQL can omit unused space or compress images.
design: Leave torn-page protection enabled unless the storage stack guarantees atomic page writes. Watch image bytes when increasing checkpoint frequency.

short: The elapsed-time trigger for automatic WAL checkpoints.
detail: Automatic checkpoints can also start earlier due to WAL volume. Production PostgreSQL uses seconds or minutes. The lab uses subsecond intervals to make the sequence easy to observe.
design: Set the interval with recovery-time goals and steady-state I/O in mind. Shorter intervals can increase full-page image frequency.

short: A soft WAL-volume limit used to trigger automatic checkpoints.
detail: PostgreSQL can exceed it while a checkpoint runs, during spikes, or when slots and archiving retain old files. The chart displays generated record sizes. The disk meter measures reserved segment bytes.
design: Tune checkpoint pressure with max_wal_size, and alert separately on actual pg_wal disk usage and retention blockers.

short: The fraction of the checkpoint interval used as a pacing target for automatic checkpoint writes.
detail: A value near 0.9 spreads the writes across most of the expected interval. A smaller value concentrates work. Changes in WAL generation or I/O pressure can alter actual progress.
design: A smoother write profile reduces spikes in foreground I/O contention. Track checkpoint write and sync time under realistic load.

short: The positions the primary has sent and the standby has written to its OS.
detail: sent_lsn is reported by the sender. write_lsn is the position reported written by the standby. Locally, write LSN similarly refers to WAL delivered to the OS before a durable flush.
design: Compare sent and write positions to isolate network and receive-side delays before looking at flush latency or replay.

short: The WAL endpoint made durable by a storage synchronization operation.
detail: The primary and standby have separate flush positions. For a synchronous standby, synchronous_commit on waits for the standby’s reported flush.
design: A received or written record may still be lost if the standby itself crashes. Use the flush position for remote durability guarantees.

short: The position up to which the standby has applied WAL to its database state.
detail: Replay can lag behind receipt and durable flush. remote_apply requires the standby to replay the commit record before the primary acknowledges the commit.
design: Monitor replay progress when serving reads on standby. Receipt and storage metrics alone cannot quantify stale reads.

short: The oldest WAL position that the replication slot’s consumer may still need.
detail: Physical standby feedback advances it with durable receive progress in this lab. A logical slot’s restart_lsn can lag its confirmed_flush_lsn because decoding needs earlier WAL.
design: Use the byte distance from current WAL to restart_lsn to size retention exposure. An active consumer can still pin substantial history.

short: How far a standby is behind the primary at a chosen stage of replication.
detail: This lab reports the byte gap between primary flush and standby replay. Sent, write and flush positions help locate where the gap is accumulating.
design: Use byte lag for backlog size and elapsed lag for user-facing staleness. Alert on the stage tied to the guarantee your application needs.

short: The setting that selects which connected standbys may be required for synchronous commit.
detail: It can choose prioritized or quorum acknowledgement. The lab uses one named standby. If it is unavailable, commits requiring remote acknowledgement can wait.
design: Make the availability and durability trade-off explicit. A synchronous topology needs enough reachable standbys to satisfy its acknowledgement rule.

short: A checkpoint-time limit on how much WAL a slot can retain.
detail: The default of −1 permits unlimited slot retention. When the limit leaves required segments eligible for removal, an affected slot can become unusable. Other retention requirements can still keep files on disk.
design: Set a budget with outage and recovery windows in mind. A cap trades automatic catch-up for primary disk headroom and must be paired with lag monitoring.

short: Restoring a base backup and replaying archived WAL up to a chosen point.
detail: Recovery requires a continuous WAL chain from the backup to the target and the correct timeline. The base backup is the initial physical copy, and the archive fills in later changes.
design: PITR can recover from logical mistakes that immediately replicate. Validate archive continuity and practice a timed restore.

short: Turning WAL into a stream of logical changes that downstream applications can consume.
detail: Logical decoding assembles committed changes from WAL, and CDC means change data capture. A logical slot retains WAL needed to restart decoding after a disconnect.
design: Plan for consumer backpressure and replay. A stalled CDC pipeline can threaten the primary’s disk even when its physical standbys are healthy.
